title: Chapter 14 — Nantucket
paragraphs: Nothing else noteworthy happened during the crossing, so after a fine run, we arrived safely in Nantucket.

Nantucket! Take out your map and look at it. See what a real corner of the world it occupies; how it stands there, far offshore, lonelier than the Eddystone lighthouse. Look at it — a mere hillock, an elbow of sand; all beach, with no background. There is more sand there than you would use in twenty years as a substitute for blotting paper. Some playful fellows will tell you that they have to plant weeds there, since they don't grow naturally; that they import Canada thistles; that they have to send overseas for a wooden plug to stop a leak in an oil cask; that pieces of wood in Nantucket are carried about like bits of the true cross in Rome; that people there plant toadstools in front of their houses, to get under the shade in summertime; that one blade of grass makes an oasis, and three blades in a day's walk a prairie; that they wear quicksand shoes, something like Laplander snowshoes; that they are so shut in, belted about, enclosed every way, surrounded, and made an utter island of by the ocean, that small clams will sometimes be found sticking to their very chairs and tables, as to the backs of sea turtles. But these extravaganzas only show that Nantucket is no Illinois.

Now consider the marvelous traditional story of how the red men came to settle this island. The legend goes like this. Long ago an eagle swooped down on the New England coast and carried off an Indian baby in his talons. Wailing loudly, the parents watched their child carried away out of sight over the wide waters. They decided to follow in the same direction. They set out in their canoes, and after a dangerous crossing they found the island, and there they found an empty ivory casket — the poor little Indian's skeleton.

What wonder, then, that these Nantucketers, born on a beach, should take to the sea for a living! First they caught crabs and quahogs in the sand; grown bolder, they waded out with nets for mackerel; more experienced, they pushed off in boats and caught cod; and at last, launching a navy of great ships on the sea, they explored this watery world, put an unceasing belt of circumnavigations around it, peeped in at the Bering Strait, and in all seasons and all oceans declared everlasting war on the mightiest animated mass that has survived the flood — most monstrous and most mountainous! That Himalayan, salt-sea Mastodon, clothed with such an ominous weight of unconscious power that his very panics are more to be dreaded than his most fearless and malicious attacks!

And so these naked Nantucketers, these hermits of the sea, swarming out of their anthill in the ocean, have overrun and conquered the watery world like so many Alexanders, carving up the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans among themselves the way the three pirate powers carved up Poland. Let America add Mexico to Texas and stack Cuba on top of Canada; let the English swarm over all of India and hang their blazing flag from the sun; two thirds of this globe of land and water belong to the Nantucketer. For the sea is his; he owns it as emperors own empires, while other seamen have only a right of way through it. Merchant ships are nothing but extension bridges; warships nothing but floating forts; even pirates and privateers, though they follow the sea the way highwaymen follow the road, only rob other ships — other fragments of the land like themselves — without trying to make their living from the bottomless deep itself. The Nantucketer alone lives and revels on the sea; he alone, in the Bible's words, goes down to it in ships, plowing it back and forth as his own private plantation. That is his home; that is where his business lies, a business that Noah's flood would not interrupt, even if it drowned all the millions in China. He lives on the sea as prairie chickens live on the prairie; he hides among the waves, and he climbs them the way chamois hunters climb the Alps. For years at a time he doesn't know the land, so that when he finally reaches it, it smells like another world, stranger than the moon would smell to an earthling. Like the landless gull, which folds her wings at sunset and is rocked to sleep between the swells, the Nantucketer at nightfall, out of sight of land, furls his sails and lies down to rest, while under his very pillow herds of walruses and whales rush past.
